ideas.name: What Bigdata is and where it comes from

en.text: Emerging technologies are new or evolving technologies expected within five to ten years with big social or economic effects. Bigdata is one of them: data sets so massive and complex that typical data processing software and database tools cannot easily process them. It comes from business transactions, IoT devices, social media, smartphone locations and surveys. An organization identifies its sources, then builds a pipeline that moves the data to storage for use.

en.text: Bigdata is characterized by five V's. Volume is the huge amount of data. Variety is its many forms: structured (spreadsheets, relational databases), unstructured (audio, images, text, video) and semi-structured (JSON, XML, HTML). Velocity is the speed at which data is created in real time. Veracity is how reliable the data is. Value is the useful, trustworthy data that gives insights.

en.text: Bigdata helps companies win and keep customers, target advertisements, develop products, set the best prices, manage risks and make better decisions. In Ethiopia, Ethiopian Airlines, Ethio Telecom, the Artificial Intelligence Center and some banks use it to serve and segment customers. It is applied in healthcare, education, banking (real-time fraud detection), agriculture, manufacturing, retail and transportation. Each application follows one pattern: data sources, then analytics, then a better service.

en.text: Bigdata also has challenges. Data grows quickly, so storing and managing it is hard. Companies lack skilled data scientists, data analysts and data engineers. Huge data stores must be secured, otherwise they can become a haven for intruders. Data comes from many sources, so it must be integrated and the most relevant data chosen. Data quality and validation are further challenges.

notes.text: p.31: "tectarget.com" is a typo for techtarget.com; the lesson uses the correct name.

p.33: the book's "Price optimization" text does not say what it is. The lesson teaches the fuller meaning: analysing sales, demand and competitor data to set the best price, with less manual work and fewer errors.
p.37: "unless it serve as a haven for intruders" should read "otherwise they may serve as a haven for intruders"; the lesson uses the corrected meaning.
Brainstorming 2.2 is used twice in this unit (Benefits of Bigdata and Cloud Computing). The lesson cites the Bigdata box as Brainstorming 2.2.
Ethiopian examples (telebirr, Ethio Telecom records, Hawassa supermarket, Bahir Dar farmer, Ethiopian Airlines data mix) and the V-scenario items are added and marked.
